proposal.utterance: Classify 'Abusus' (the right of abuse, in Roman-law property theory) in BFO terms.

entities.label: Abusus
entities.rationale: Abusus is a kind of legal right (specifically the right to alienate or destroy property) recognized within a legal system. As a right, it is externally grounded in a social-legal practice (Roman property law and its successors), inhering in a bearer (the dominus/owner) and dependent on institutional recognition. It is therefore a Role (BFO_0000023), and since LegalRight is already modeled as a subclass of BFO_0000023 in the working ontology, Abusus is most precisely a subclass of LegalRight. It is a class (kind) because it denotes a type of right that multiple owners can bear, not a single individual instance.

relations.rationale: Abusus is a species of LegalRight (itself a subclass of BFO_0000023 Role), inheriting both the role character and the legal-right character already modeled in the working ontology.

open_questions: Should Abusus be restricted to Roman-law contexts (a historical legal right class), or should it also cover civil-law systems that inherited the tripartite usus/fructus/abusus scheme? This affects whether we mint a single class or a hierarchy.
Do you want to model usus and fructus as sibling classes under LegalRight as well, to capture the full Roman-law dominium structure?

Should we assert that Abusus inheres in a bearer class (e.g., PropertyOwner as a Role) and add a corresponding disposition or condition (LegalExistenceCondition / NormOntologicalCondition) that grounds it? This would make the relational structure more complete.

Is 'Abusus' intended here as a class (the kind of right) or as a specific individual right-token within a particular legal system such as Roman law? If the latter, it should be typed as an individual of class LegalRight or Abusus-class.
proposal.rationale_summary: Abusus—the ius abutendi or right of abuse in Roman and civil-law property theory—is the component of dominium that entitles the owner to alienate, consume, or destroy the thing owned. Ontologically it is a specifically dependent continuant: it cannot exist without a bearer (the owner of the res) and without institutional grounding in a legal system. BFO's Role (BFO_0000023) is the correct high-level type because the right is externally grounded in social-legal practice rather than in the intrinsic physical constitution of the bearer (which would point to Disposition). The working ontology already has LegalRight as a subclass of BFO_0000023, so Abusus is most economically introduced as a subclass of LegalRight, capturing that it is a species of legally recognized entitlement. It is modeled as a class rather than an individual because it denotes a recurrent kind of right that different owners instantiate across legal systems and time periods.
